A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CaT/CFCN research and are readable throughout, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices. Retitling, reorganization, and the additional appendix sections do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations, CaT/CFCN evaluations on Twins and Jobs, architectural comparisons, and a secondary analysis of psychology data.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds random-forest/transformer benchmark results and CaT/CFCN evaluations on ACIC 2016.

M1.justification: The architectures, masking equations, CFCN-mod, and recursive Algorithm 1 are retained. However, new S13 describes intervention effects propagating in a single forward pass, conflicting with the recursive procedure retained in Sections 3.5 and S6. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents an intended inference revision or an inconsistent theoretical description.

E1.justification: S12 adds ACIC 2016, covering 77 data-generating processes and evaluating individual treatment-effect accuracy through PEHE. The toy simulation, Twins, Jobs, and psychology application remain. v1 mentions IHDP without providing corresponding results or experimental details, so dropping those mentions does not establish removal of an evaluated dataset.

E2.justification: Table 7 adds ordinary transformers and random forests to the Twins/Jobs comparisons; previously they appeared only in the motivating simulation. ACIC Table 8 also introduces evaluated comparators including Causal Tree, DR-CFR, and TEDVAE. Newly discussed DML and IPW are not reported experimental comparators.

E3.justification: The added ACIC evaluation introduces a 60/30/10 train/validation/test split, explicitly forgoes validation-based tuning, and evaluates within- and out-of-sample PEHE. Its CaT configuration uses three layers, five heads, and input embedding dimension 20. These are settings for a new evaluation, rather than demonstrated changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: The incorrect-DAG and covariate-shift experiments, CFCN-mod comparison, negative isomorphic-shuffling finding, and psychology case study are retained. The new appendix tables add benchmark comparisons, without a new ablation, perturbation, robustness test, or error-analysis protocol.

E5.justification: Both versions report 30 motivating simulations, 100 Jobs runs with shared seeds across models, and 100 psychology bootstrap repetitions using a 0.9 sampling fraction. Standard-deviation and standard-error reporting practices remain unchanged; additional result rows do not establish a new statistical procedure or increased replication.

E6.justification: Existing numerical tables and result plots are retained, but Tables 7–8 add substantial results. Table 7 reports Twins out-of-sample eATE of 0.0072 for the transformer and 0.0084 for random forest. On newly evaluated ACIC, out-of-sample PEHE is 4.26 for CaT and 4.17 for CFCN, versus 1.79 for random forest and 1.77 for TEDVAE. These are new comparisons, not same-setting performance changes from v1.

T1.justification: S8 adds one-step potential outcomes, recursive substitution, adjustment-set identification, and explicit ignorability, positivity, and SUTVA assumptions. New S13 introduces architectural assumptions, propositions, a lemma, two theorems, and a corollary concerning parental dependence, DAG factorization, interventions, robustness, and transportability. v1 contains no corresponding formal development.

C1.justification: v1 presents CFCN and CaT as two principal contributions. v4's title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion center CaT and recast CFCN as an architectural baseline. The conclusion also newly claims complementarity with DML and IPW through use as plug-in estimators.

C2.justification: S12 expands the earlier brief benchmark caveat into a substantive argument that shared simple DAG assumptions allow standard estimators to compete strongly, motivating benchmarks involving discovery or feature selection. Causal-identification and robustness assumptions become explicit. The explanation for omitting layer normalization changes from cross-variable information leakage to rescaling calibrated interventions; existing recursion, DAG-availability, and scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 supplies ACIC access information and its specific CaT hyperparameters, and explicitly describes the confounder-graph assumption used for Twins and Jobs. Existing implementation descriptions, hyperparameter tables, data-processing instructions, and promises concerning code release are largely retained.

R1.justification: The nearest-work discussion expands beyond MADE to Graphical Normalizing Flows and Structured Neural Networks, helping reposition CFCN as a simple architectural baseline. v4 also adds substantial causal-identification literature and positions the models as complementary to DML/IPW rather than solely as standalone causal architectures.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. CaT now precedes CFCN in the methods section, contribution terminology changes throughout, and the appendix narrative expands to S12–S13. These changes substantially reorganize the presentation of retained material.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format, with widespread resizing and relocation of displays. The former main-text Figure 2 moves to appendix Figure 5, while the architecture diagram becomes Figure 2. Tables 7–8 are added; existing result plots are retained rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: The added baseline comparisons, ACIC results showing weaker CaT/CFCN performance, and explicit causal assumptions improve empirical coverage and qualification. However, S13 newly asserts guarantees that are not supported by the displayed mechanics: zeroing logits before softmax does not eliminate attention, and claimed single-pass intervention propagation conflicts with recursive Algorithm 1. These material theoretical inconsistencies coexist with useful empirical additions, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
